items.title: Human Evolution
items.body:
## Human Evolution

- **Australopithecus** — a group of hominins that lived from **4.4 million to 1.4 million years ago**; regarded as close ancestors of modern humans.
- **Homo habilis** — the earliest member of the genus *Homo*, lived in sub-Saharan Africa between **2 and 1.5 million years ago**.
- **Homo erectus** — the 'missing link' between humans and apes; the first fossil was discovered on **Java Island in 1891**. In India, the earliest evidence was found in the **Narmada Valley** (*Homo erectus narmadensis*).
- **Homo sapiens neanderthalensis** (Neanderthal man) — fossils first discovered in **Germany in 1856**.
- **Homo sapiens** — the modern upright-walking species evolved in **Africa around 315,000 years ago**; the oldest modern *Homo sapiens sapiens* fossils were found at **Cro-Magnon, France** (~100,000–125,000 B.P.).

figure.alt: Sequence of human evolution from Australopithecus afarensis to Homo sapiens
figure.caption: Australopithecus → Homo habilis → Homo erectus → Homo neanderthalensis → Homo sapiens.

keyPoints: Australopithecus (4.4–1.4 mya) — close ancestor of modern humans.
Homo erectus first fossil found on Java Island (1891); in India in the Narmada Valley (narmadensis).
Neanderthal fossils first found in Germany (1856).
Homo sapiens evolved in Africa ~315,000 years ago; oldest sapiens sapiens at Cro-Magnon, France.
items.mnemonic: Evolution order "Aha! Every New Species": Australopithecus → Homo habilis → Erectus → Neanderthal → Sapiens.
items.source: local APPSC GK PDF — Ancient History: Stone Age (Human Evolution)

items.title: Stone Age — Overview & Periodisation
items.body:
## Pre-Historic Period or Stone Age

- The Stone Age is a **prehistoric cultural stage** defined by the creation and use of **stone tools**.
- It began with the first appearance of **hominids** and lasted until the **development of agriculture**.
- The archaeological system based on the Stone Age was developed by **Christian Jurgensen Thomson in 1820**.
- It is divided into **three major periods**:
  1. **Palaeolithic Age** — hunters and food gatherers (up to 10,000 BC).
  2. **Mesolithic Age** — transition between Palaeolithic and Neolithic.
  3. **Neolithic Age** — food producers (4000–1000 BC).
- The later **Chalcolithic (Copper) Age** (3500–1000 BC) marks the transition out of the pure Stone Age.

figure.alt: Timeline chart of prehistoric cultures in India: Palaeolithic, Mesolithic, Neolithic, Chalcolithic, Iron Age
figure.caption: Prehistoric cultures in India and their approximate date ranges.

keyPoints: Stone Age = prehistoric stage defined by stone tools.
Archaeological three-age system devised by Christian Jurgensen Thomson (1820).
Three major periods: Palaeolithic → Mesolithic → Neolithic.
Chalcolithic (Copper) Age follows, marking the exit from the Stone Age.
items.mnemonic: Sequence "Please Mind Nature's Copper" = Palaeolithic → Mesolithic → Neolithic → Chalcolithic.
items.source: local APPSC GK PDF — Ancient History: Stone Age (Pre-Historic Period or Stone Age)

items.title: Palaeolithic Age (up to 10,000 BC)
items.body:
## Palaeolithic Age

- The term **Palaeolithic** was introduced by **John Lubbock in 1865** to describe the period when early humans used stone tools made of **quartzite** — hence they are called **Quartzite Men**.
- This period corresponds with the **Pleistocene (Ice Age)**.
- People lived by **hunting and food gathering** and did **not** know pottery, agriculture, or metals.
- It is divided into three sub-periods by tool technology and climate:
  1. **Lower Palaeolithic** (up to 100,000 BC) — hand axes, cleavers, choppers, chopping tools.
  2. **Middle Palaeolithic** (100,000–40,000 BC) — flake/pebble tools; blades, points, borers dominant.
  3. **Upper Palaeolithic** (40,000–10,000 BC) — burins, scrapers, a developed flint industry; emergence of modern *Homo sapiens*.
keyPoints: 'Palaeolithic' coined by John Lubbock (1865); people called Quartzite Men.
Coincides with the Pleistocene / Ice Age.
No pottery, agriculture or metals — pure hunting-gathering.
Three sub-periods: Lower (up to 100,000 BC), Middle (100,000–40,000 BC), Upper (40,000–10,000 BC).
items.mnemonic: Tools by phase "Lower Hands, Middle Blades, Upper Burins": hand-axes → blades/points/borers → burins/scrapers.
items.source: local APPSC GK PDF — Ancient History: Stone Age (Palaeolithic Age; Lower/Middle/Upper Palaeolithic)

items.title: Palaeolithic Sites of India
items.body:
## Key Palaeolithic Sites

- **Lower Palaeolithic:** Belan Valley (MP/UP), **Bhimbetka** (MP), Bagor & Budha Pushkar (Rajasthan), Renugunta & **Kurnool Caves** (Andhra Pradesh), Singhbhum (Jharkhand), **Sohan Valley** (West Punjab, Pakistan).
- **Middle Palaeolithic:** Nevasa (Maharashtra), Bhimbetka & **Narmada Valley** (MP), Didwana & Bagor (Rajasthan), Singhbhum (Jharkhand). The **Belan Valley** was rich in both stone tools and animal fossils.
- **Upper Palaeolithic:** Kurnool Caves (AP), Belan Valley, Sabarmati Valley (Gujarat), **Attirampakkam** (Tamil Nadu), Hunsgi Valley (Karnataka), **Hathnora** (Narmada Valley), Adamgarh (MP).
- **Bhimbetka Rock Shelter** (MP) is one of the largest prehistoric complexes and was inscribed as a **UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2003**.
- **Bone tools** were found only at the **Kurnool** cave sites (Upper Palaeolithic).

figure.alt: Map of Palaeolithic sites of India including Bhimbetka, Kurnool, Attirampakkam and Belan Valley
figure.caption: Distribution of major Palaeolithic sites across India.

keyPoints: Bhimbetka (MP) — largest prehistoric complex; UNESCO World Heritage Site.
Belan Valley yielded stone tools and animal fossils across Lower and Middle phases.
Kurnool Caves (AP) — bone tools found only here (Upper Palaeolithic).
Sohan Valley (Pakistan) and Attirampakkam (TN) are landmark Palaeolithic sites.
items.mnemonic: Andhra Palaeolithic caves = "Kurnool Keeps Bones" — the only bone-tool site.
items.source: local APPSC GK PDF — Ancient History: Stone Age (Lower/Middle/Upper Palaeolithic Age Sites)

items.title: Prominent Pre-Historic Archaeologists in India
items.body:
## Pioneers of Indian Pre-History

- **Sir Alexander Cunningham** — the **first Director of the Archaeological Survey of India (AD 1861)**; played a pivotal role in discovering Palaeolithic sites.
- **Robert Bruce Foote** — known as the **Father of Indian Pre-history**; he discovered the **Pallavaram Hand Axe** and made major contributions to prehistoric studies.
keyPoints: Alexander Cunningham — first Director of the ASI (AD 1861).
Robert Bruce Foote — 'Father of Indian Pre-history'.
Foote discovered the Pallavaram Hand Axe.
items.source: local APPSC GK PDF — Ancient History: Stone Age (Prominent Archaeologists in Pre-Historical Studies in India)

items.title: Mesolithic Age (9000–4000 BC)
items.body:
## Mesolithic Age

- Marks the **transition** between the Palaeolithic and Neolithic ages; belongs to the **Holocene Era** (after the Pleistocene Ice Age).
- Defining feature: **microliths** — small, sharp stone tools (~1–2 cm) of **flint or chert**, often mounted on wooden shafts to make **spears, harpoons and arrows**.
- **Lifestyle:** early nomadic hunter-gatherers → herders (domesticating dogs, sheep, goats) → early farming of wheat and barley towards the end.
- **Art:** the **Bhimbetka caves** (MP) contain rock paintings of hunting, food gathering, dancing and daily life.
- **Domestication:** evidence of cows, horses and poultry at **Adamgarh** and **Bagor**.
- **Pottery:** began at **Sanganakallu** (Karnataka) — handmade dull-brown/black ware.
- **Burials:** at **Damdama** (UP), three human skeletons were found in a single grave.
keyPoints: Transition age of the Holocene; defined by microliths (1–2 cm flint/chert tools).
Microliths hafted onto shafts → spears, harpoons, arrows.
Adamgarh & Bagor — early animal domestication; Sanganakallu — earliest pottery.
Bhimbetka — rich Mesolithic rock art; Damdama — three skeletons in one grave.
items.mnemonic: Mesolithic marker = MICRO: tiny hafted tools for the MICRO-era between Old and New Stone Age.
items.source: local APPSC GK PDF — Ancient History: Stone Age (Mesolithic Age; Art; Domestication; Pottery; Burial Practices)

items.title: Neolithic Age — Food Producers (4000–1000 BC)
items.body:
## Neolithic Age (New Stone Age)

- Marked a shift from **hunting-gathering to agriculture and animal husbandry**.
- Defined by **polished stone tools**, domestication of plants and animals, and **permanent settlements**.
- **Crops:** wheat, barley, ragi, horse gram and cotton; **animals:** cattle, sheep, goats, pigs.
- **Mehrgarh** (Balochistan, Pakistan) is the **oldest known Neolithic site** in the Indian subcontinent, dating to **7000 BC**.
- **Settlements:** mud-brick houses (rectangular/circular); **Burzahom** (Kashmir) reveals **pit dwellings** with plastered mud walls.
keyPoints: New Stone Age: agriculture + animal husbandry + permanent settlements.
Polished stone tools are the hallmark.
Mehrgarh (Balochistan) — oldest Neolithic site, c. 7000 BC.
Burzahom (Kashmir) — famous for pit dwellings.
items.mnemonic: Neolithic crops "We Buy Ragi Horse Cotton" = Wheat, Barley, Ragi, Horse gram, Cotton.
items.source: local APPSC GK PDF — Ancient History: Stone Age (Neolithic Age; Agriculture and Domestication; Settlements)

items.title: Neolithic Developments & Sites
items.body:
## Other Neolithic Developments

- **Pottery:** invented in this age — handmade, fire-baked; used for storage and cooking. Types include **grey ware, black-burnished ware and mat-impressed ware**.
- **Polished stone tools:** axes, sickles and blades for agriculture and domestic use.
- **Wheel and fire:** the invention of the **wheel** and the controlled use of **fire** transformed transport, cooking and tool-making.
- **Social structure:** food surplus led to **granaries, storage pits** and early settled/urban culture.
- **Religion:** burials indicate a belief in an **afterlife**; at **Burzahom**, domestic dogs were buried alongside humans.
- **Chirand** (Bihar) is notable for its **bone tools and weapons**.

### Notable sites
- Kashmir: **Burzahom, Gufkral**; Assam: **Daojali Hading**; UP: Chopani Mando, Mahagarha; Bihar: **Chirand**, Chechar.
- Karnataka: **Tekkalakota, Sanganakallu, Hallur, Brahmagiri, Maski/Kupgal**; Andhra: **Nagarjunakonda, Piklihal, Utnur**; Tamil Nadu: Paiyampalli.
keyPoints: Pottery invented — grey ware, black-burnished ware, mat-impressed ware.
Invention of the wheel and controlled use of fire.
Burzahom — dogs buried with humans (belief in afterlife).
Chirand (Bihar) — famous for bone tools and weapons.
items.mnemonic: Neolithic firsts = "Wheel, Fire, Pottery, Polish" — the four technologies of the New Stone Age.
items.source: local APPSC GK PDF — Ancient History: Stone Age (Other Developments; Neolithic Age Sites)

items.title: Pre-Historic Art
items.body:
## Pre-Historic Art

- Artistic expressions included **cave paintings, rock engravings and miniature figurative carvings**.
- Made from readily available materials — **ochre, burnt wood and cave walls**.
- **Bhimbetka (MP), Belan Valley (UP) and Narmada Valley** are known for prehistoric art spanning **all three phases** of the Stone Age.
- Paintings depicted **man, animals and geometric patterns**, with scenes of **hunting and family life**.
keyPoints: Forms: cave paintings, rock engravings, miniature carvings.
Media: ochre, burnt wood, cave walls.
Bhimbetka, Belan Valley and Narmada Valley span all three Stone Age phases.
Themes: humans, animals, geometric patterns, hunting and family life.
items.source: local APPSC GK PDF — Ancient History: Stone Age (Pre-Historic Art)

items.title: Chalcolithic Age (3500–1000 BC)
items.body:
## Chalcolithic Age (Copper Age)

- Period when humans began using **copper and bronze** for tools — also called the **Copper Age**.
- Cultures existed in the **Chhota Nagpur Plateau, Upper Gangetic Basin, Karnataka** and along the **Narmada**.
- People lived in **thatched mud-brick houses** and practised **Jhum (shifting) cultivation**.
- **Ganeshwar** (Rajasthan) was a major site of copper artifacts, related to the **Jodhpura culture**.
- **Pottery:** **Black and Red Ware (BRW)** — wheel-made and brightly coloured — was the signature.
- **Ornaments** of agate, jasper, chalcedony and carnelian; **crops** included green gram, lentil, grass pea, black gram, rice and wheat.
- **Social structure:** village chiefs lived in large rectangular houses — an early sign of **social inequality**.
keyPoints: Copper Age — first use of copper and bronze tools.
Signature pottery: Black and Red Ware (BRW), wheel-made.
Ganeshwar (Rajasthan) — major copper-artifact site, Jodhpura culture.
Large chiefs' houses — early evidence of social inequality.
items.mnemonic: Chalco = 'copper'; remember "Copper + BRW" as the two Chalcolithic hallmarks.
items.source: local APPSC GK PDF — Ancient History: Stone Age (Chalcolithic Age; Key Features of Chalcolithic Culture)

items.title: Chalcolithic Cultures
items.body:
## Major Chalcolithic Cultures

- **Ahar-Banas** (3000–1500 BC, Rajasthan) — known for **Black and Red Ware (BRW)**; adjacent to the Indus Valley Civilization.
- **Kayatha** (2400–2000 BC, MP) — **earliest agricultural settlement** in the Malwa region.
- **Malwa** (1600–1300 BC) — key sites Navdatoli, Eran and Nagda; **Navdatoli** was the largest.
- **Savalda** (2000–1800 BC) — influenced by Mesolithic cultures in northern Maharashtra and Harappans in Gujarat.
- **Jorwe** (1400–700 BC, Maharashtra) — black/red-painted pottery and a **blade-flake industry using chalcedony**.
- **Prabhas and Rangpur** (2000–1400 BC) — derived from the Harappan Civilization; known for **Lustrous Red Ware**.
keyPoints: Ahar-Banas — BRW, adjacent to the IVC.
Kayatha — earliest agricultural settlement of Malwa.
Jorwe — blade-flake industry using chalcedony.
Prabhas & Rangpur — Harappan-derived Lustrous Red Ware.
items.mnemonic: Cultures "A Kind Man Sees Jolly Prabhas" = Ahar, Kayatha, Malwa, Savalda, Jorwe, Prabhas-Rangpur.
items.source: local APPSC GK PDF — Ancient History: Stone Age (Chalcolithic Cultures)

items.title: Megalithic Culture & Burial Practices
items.body:
## Megalithic Culture in South India

- Characterised by **large stone monuments** used for burial and ritual.
- **Iron artifacts** were common at Megalithic sites, and **tank irrigation** was introduced, revolutionising South Indian agriculture.
- Burials used stone boxes called **cists**, with grave goods reflecting **social status**.
- **Sangam literature** describes South Indian burial practices, some persisting among the **Maria Gonds (Chhattisgarh), Bondos (Odisha) and Khasis (Assam)**.
- **Sites:** Junapani (Maharashtra), Adichanallur & Kodumanal (Tamil Nadu), Brahmagiri & Sanganakallu (Karnataka).
keyPoints: Megalithic = large stone burial/ritual monuments, associated with iron.
Introduced tank irrigation in South India.
Dead buried in stone boxes called cists; grave goods signal status.
Sites: Junapani, Adichanallur, Brahmagiri, Kodumanal, Sanganakallu.
items.mnemonic: Megalithic burial box = CIST (think 'chest' of stone).
items.source: local APPSC GK PDF — Ancient History: Stone Age (Megalithic Culture in South India; Burial Practices During the Stone Age)

items.title: Exam-Frequent Sites, Pairs & Facts
items.body:
## High-Frequency PYQ Facts

### Site – State – Type (match traps)
| Site | State | Association |
|---|---|---|
| **Inamgaon** | Maharashtra | Largest **Jorwe (Chalcolithic)** settlement on Ghod river |
| **Chandraketugarh** | **West Bengal** (not Odisha) | **Terracotta** art (early historic) |
| **Mangadu** | Kerala | **Megalithic** site |
| **Salihundam** | Andhra Pradesh | **Buddhist** stupa site (not rock-cut) |
| **Bairat** | Rajasthan | **Buddhist** remains (Ashokan) |
| **Atranjikhera** | **Uttar Pradesh** (not Rajasthan) | **OCP** (Ochre Coloured Pottery) culture |
| **Chirand** | Bihar | Neolithic bone tools |
| **Ahar (Aahar)** | Rajasthan (near **Udaipur**) | Chalcolithic **BRW** |
| **Rangpur** | Gujarat | Late-Harappan Lustrous Red Ware |

### Earliest agriculture / ‘firsts’
- Earliest cultivated rice in India: **Belan valley** sites — **Koldihwa, Mahagara, Tokwa, Lahuradeva** (UP). Lahuradeva is now cited as among the **oldest rice (~6400 BCE)**.
- **Mehrgarh** (Bolan Pass, Balochistan) — called the **‘Bread Basket’ / cradle of farming**; **first permanent settlements** (Neolithic) with mud-brick houses.
- Animal **domestication began in the Mesolithic** (Adamgarh, Bagor).

### Other tested facts
- **Most rock paintings** belong to the **Upper Palaeolithic**, with **highest density in the Mesolithic** (Bhimbetka).
- **Ahar–Banas** long-distance trade is shown by **Lapis Lazuli** (imported from Afghanistan).
- **Halbi, Ho and Kui** are **tribal languages** (Austro-Asiatic/Dravidian) — not Stone-Age cultures.
- **Kalibangan** (Rajasthan) = Mature Harappan; **Bagor** (Rajasthan) = largest **Mesolithic** site.
keyPoints: Inamgaon (Maharashtra) = largest Jorwe Chalcolithic site; Chandraketugarh = WB terracotta.
Atranjikhera (UP) = OCP culture, NOT Rajasthan; Ahar (near Udaipur, Rajasthan) = BRW.
Belan valley (Koldihwa/Mahagara/Tokwa/Lahuradeva) = earliest cultivated rice; Mehrgarh = 'Bread Basket'.
Most rock paintings = Upper Palaeolithic (Bhimbetka); Ahar-Banas trade shown by Lapis Lazuli.
Halbi, Ho and Kui are tribal languages, not archaeological cultures.
